html:
Gateway state publication and recovery sequences

This guide follows the local Gateway state owner from bootstrap through RAM publication, disk persistence and shutdown. The Gateway state overview describes job admission, transfer retention, runtime purge, update admission and offline operator commands. Gateway transport explains how an authenticated request reaches this owner. These are separate from the Controller's state repositories.

What each storage layer owns

GatewayRuntimeStateHub owns six record domains: jobs, transfers, Docker reservations, replay nonces, workers and policies. Callers read RAM records through copies or bounded projections. They do not fall back to a database when a record is absent. A checkpoint saves an immutable view of those domains; independent safety records preserve selected facts even when that checkpoint is older than the live state.

flowchart TD Callers[Job, transfer, Docker, authentication and worker callers] --> Tx[Optimistic RAM transactions] Tx --> Roots[Six immutable domain roots and record revisions] Tx --> Indexes[Active, resource, GPU and override indexes] Tx --> Events[1024 recent job event projections] Roots --> Reads[Copied records and bounded public projections] Roots --> Snapshot[Captured roots plus one revision] Snapshot --> Database[Complete generation state.sqlite3] Snapshot --> Setup[Independent policies and nonces setup.json] Database --> Manifest[Checksummed committed manifest] Setup --> Manifest Callers --> Fences[Dispatch, nonce, Docker and transfer safety records] Completion[Foreground or worker completion] --> Receipts[Signed terminal receipts] Retire[Explicit output retirement] --> Logs[Purged log manifest] Manifest --> Restore[Next bootstrap] Fences --> Restore Receipts --> Restore Logs --> Restore

The event deque is bounded, process-local observation history. Its sequence and owner epoch help readers follow current publications; it is not a durable journal. Events contain allowlisted job facts and bounded log previews, excluding command and environment payloads. A transaction can change another domain without producing a job event. Artifact bytes and job-output segments have separate owners.

Implementation Responsibility in these flows
hub.py Registry, leases, transactions, accounting, indexes, events and shutdown.
recovery.py Phase-guarded SQLite access, initial imports, restore and complete checkpoint generations.
fences.py Independent replay/dispatch records, receipt validation and worker-exit reconciliation.
files.py Private files, bounded reads, flushed JSON publication and lifetime leases.
indexes.py Conservative resource and uncertain-GPU candidates.
limits.py Explicit record, aggregate, job-count and active-job budgets.

Bootstrap and exclusive ownership

get_hub resolves a state root to one owner in the current process. Repeated lookups share it. A closed owner can be replaced; a quiescing owner cannot. Import bindings for Docker and replay state are restored from runtime-imports.json and cannot be changed after the owner reaches READY.

sequenceDiagram participant Caller participant Registry as Process registry participant Hub as New state hub participant Files as Private files and leases participant Recovery participant Fences as Safety evidence Caller->>Registry: get_hub(root, import bindings) alt Existing live owner with matching bindings Registry-->>Caller: Shared hub else New or previously closed owner Registry->>Hub: Construct under registry lock Hub->>Files: Acquire root lease and optional replay-root lease Hub->>Files: Retain import bindings and node identity Hub->>Files: Acquire machine-local node lease Hub->>Recovery: Restore committed generation or initial imports Recovery-->>Hub: Domain roots and revision Hub->>Hub: Enter RECONCILING Hub->>Fences: Restore fences, receipts and log retirements Hub->>Files: Establish initial process-ownership evidence if absent Hub->>Hub: Check record, total-byte and job-count limits Hub->>Hub: Rebuild indexes and enter READY Hub->>Recovery: Start background checkpointer Registry-->>Caller: Ready hub end Note over Hub,Files: Bootstrap failure releases acquired leases and propagates

The root lease rejects another process using the same directory. The node lease also rejects a copied root with the same node identity on the same machine. When configured, replay state has its own leased directory and identity. The random owner epoch changes with a new hub; it is distinct from the persisted node identity and the runtime-purge epoch used by signed requests.

Fork handling closes the child's inherited lease handles without explicitly unlocking the parent's authority and clears its registry. A stale hub object also rejects access from a different PID. Private-file validation rejects linked final paths, unexpected file types, multiple hard links and unsuitable ownership or permissions; Windows uses its ACL helper. Directory creation checks the target and missing ancestors, rather than recursively validating every existing ancestor.

Restore validates the manifest version, node, domain set, generation name, revision, database checksum and SQLite integrity. Older manifests without the policies domain are accepted through the defined compatibility path. Before the first initialization, missing recovery state can import the bound legacy stores. After the initialized marker exists, a missing manifest fails startup. Corrupt committed state does not automatically select the previous generation. The offline repair command makes that choice explicitly under exclusive ownership.

One RAM transaction

Transactions capture persistent roots and indexes under a short lock. Reads return deep copies and track the exact observed cells, including absent records. A blind write first records its old cell, so it still conflicts with a concurrent change. Candidate or override scans additionally depend on the admission-index revision.

sequenceDiagram participant Caller as Pure state operation participant Tx as Transaction participant Hub as RAM owner participant IPC as Worker authority Caller->>Tx: Begin Tx->>Hub: Capture roots and indexes under lock Caller->>Tx: Read copies, compute and stage writes Tx->>Tx: Drop unchanged writes, encode sizes and prepare events Tx->>Hub: Acquire publication lock Hub->>Hub: Validate owner, observed cells and scanned index revision alt Observation changed Hub-->>Caller: Conflict with no publication Note over Caller,Tx: Retry pure computation with a fresh transaction else Capacity or new-job admission denied Hub-->>Caller: Error with no publication else Valid changes Hub->>Hub: Publish roots, indexes, accounting, dirty revisions and events Hub->>Hub: Notify condition waiters and release lock Hub->>IPC: changed() when IPC exists Hub-->>Caller: RAM acceptance end

The retry wrapper retries only Conflict, up to 64 attempts with a short yield. Process creation, signals, filesystem operations and remote effects must remain outside retryable state work. IPC notification happens after publication and lock release. Neither a successful transaction nor a worker event acknowledgement implies that a checkpoint has completed.

Record-size checks and growth limits reject excess state rather than evicting uncertain execution evidence. New jobs require READY. Existing records remain accessible during QUIESCING so owners can finish state transitions and persistence. The budget table lists the exact settings. Bootstrap checks restored record bytes, total bytes and job count; the active-job limit is enforced when publication grows that active set.

An active candidate includes a terminal job when historical effects remain uncertain or reconciliation is required. Missing resource classification uses a conservative unknown bucket; trusted read-only classifications can avoid resource memberships. Candidate overlap narrows admission work but grants no permission by itself. Index changes participate in transaction conflict detection.

Checkpoint publication and concurrent changes

The background writer wakes on request or every two seconds and writes when RAM and committed revisions differ. A writer lock serializes complete generations. SQLite is permitted only in explicit BOOTSTRAP, CHECKPOINT or REPAIR phases; saved connections and cursors cannot be reused for normal runtime SQL.

sequenceDiagram participant Writer as Checkpointer participant Hub as RAM owner participant Disk as Private generation files participant Caller as Concurrent state operation Writer->>Hub: Snapshot roots and revision R Hub-->>Writer: Immutable roots at R Writer->>Disk: Write all domains into fresh state.sqlite3 Caller->>Hub: Publish newer revision R+1 Writer->>Disk: Flush database and compute checksum Writer->>Disk: Publish policies/nonces setup.json and checksum Writer->>Disk: Synchronize generation directories Writer->>Disk: Retain prior manifest as previous.json if present Writer->>Disk: Atomically publish manifest.json selecting R Note over Writer,Disk: Manifest replacement selects the committed generation Writer->>Disk: Publish initialized marker Writer->>Hub: checkpoint_complete(R, generation, timing) Hub->>Hub: Clear only dirty entries covered by R Note over Hub,Caller: R+1 remains dirty Writer->>Disk: Remove safely recognized obsolete generations

Every generation contains a complete snapshot, rather than a sequence of SQL updates. setup.json independently preserves policies and nonces for runtime purge; its checksum is recorded alongside the database checksum. Ordinary restore uses the database. Purge recovery validates the separate setup through its own workflow. Cleanup retains current and previous generations and refuses to treat unexpected directory names or contents as disposable checkpoint files.

A failure before manifest publication leaves the previous selection in place. After publication, the new generation can be recoverable even if RAM never receives its completion acknowledgement. The next bootstrap follows the manifest, while the current owner can still report dirty or degraded persistence. The background loop records an exception class and failure count and backs off before retrying. An error during old-generation cleanup can also occur after the new generation was acknowledged; failure alone does not identify which commit boundary was crossed.

Private JSON publication writes and flushes a complete encoded value, then replaces the destination and synchronizes its parent directory. Exclusive safety records instead use exclusive creation. Incomplete exclusive writes are removed; a complete record is retained if the final directory synchronization fails. This preserves uncertainty and prevents a second exclusive reservation from being accepted.

Evidence applied during recovery

Safety records are smaller than the full state and have their own publication boundaries. A dispatch fence binds the job ID, intent digest, owner epoch and accepted authorization/resource facts. It excludes the command and environment payload. Once that exclusive fence exists, another dispatch attempt is refused, including an identical attempt. A repeated public request must recover the existing operation's acknowledgement rather than reinterpret the fence as a grant.

flowchart TD Roots[Validated checkpoint or initial import roots] --> Validate[Validate safety record version, owner, category and filename] Validate --> Jobs[Check job intent matches existing record] Jobs --> Missing{Dispatched job absent?} Missing -->|Yes| Unknown[Restore unknown outcome and reconciliation requirement] Missing -->|No| Existing[Keep existing job facts] Unknown --> Merge[Merge Docker, transfer and unexpired nonce evidence] Existing --> Merge Merge --> Foreground[Validate signed foreground terminal receipts] Foreground --> Worker[Validate worker receipts against launch tickets] Worker --> Terminal[Apply consistent terminal facts only to nonterminal jobs] Terminal --> Retire[Apply purged log manifests and remove retained output fields] Retire --> Ready[Rebuild accounting and indexes before READY] Validate -->|Invalid evidence| Reject[Abort bootstrap] Foreground -->|Invalid evidence| Reject Worker -->|Invalid evidence| Reject

A job already present in the selected checkpoint is checked for intent mismatch; the fence does not unconditionally replace its state with unknown. A missing dispatched job is reconstructed conservatively with an unknown outcome and retained resource uncertainty. Docker reservations take their independent evidence; transfer records use the newer update timestamp. Expired nonce fences are discarded.

Foreground completion is published to RAM before its signed receipt is written. Worker terminal receipts use the independent launch-ticket secret and worker epoch. Both receipt paths check intent and consistent terminal facts before resolving a nonterminal job. A damaged signature or contradictory outcome cannot manufacture success. Receipt validation is distinct from output retention: retirement removes retained text from receipts and re-signs them, while purged log manifests prevent old checkpoints from resurrecting output fields.

Consuming a replay nonce

The nonce guard coordinates an in-memory pending set with exclusive disk records. It checks both retained and in-flight entries when enforcing capacity. Disk work stays outside the hub's publication mutex.

sequenceDiagram participant Auth as Authenticated-request verifier participant Fence as Nonce guard participant Hub as RAM owner participant Disk as Replay fence directory Auth->>Fence: Consume controller, nonce, time, lifetime and capacity Fence->>Fence: Under guard lock expire old entries and reserve pending ID alt Already present or pending Fence-->>Auth: gateway_request_replayed else Capacity exhausted Fence-->>Auth: gateway_nonce_capacity else Pending reservation accepted Fence->>Disk: Remove expired files and exclusively publish nonce fence alt Write or validation fails Fence-->>Auth: Replay or pairing-state error else Durable fence published Fence->>Hub: Publish nonce record Fence->>Fence: Add expiry to heap Fence-->>Auth: Nonce accepted end Fence->>Fence: Always clear pending reservation end

The independently leased replay directory can outlive a particular jobs root. Its records bind that replay identity, avoiding a reset of replay protection when the jobs owner changes. A completed exclusive write whose final directory sync failed remains reserved on disk even though the current request receives an error. The next attempt cannot infer permission from the absence of a RAM acknowledgement.

Reconciling a worker that exits after bootstrap

reconcile_worker_exit makes one receipt lookup after the supervisor exits. It does not turn ordinary status reads into disk queries. This matters when a surviving worker finishes after bootstrap but before reconnecting to the new owner.

flowchart TD Exit[Observe worker exit] --> Done{Job already terminal?} Done -->|Yes| Return[Keep existing terminal truth] Done -->|No| Receipt{Signed worker receipt present?} Receipt -->|Yes| Validate[Validate ticket, identity, intent, signature and facts] Validate --> Publish[Transaction rechecks job and publishes reconciled outcome] Publish --> Unknown{Receipt outcome unknown?} Unknown -->|Yes| Keep[Keep effect reconciliation required] Unknown -->|No| Known[Retain consistent terminal facts] Receipt -->|No| Ticket[Inspect scoped launch ticket and proven worker exit] Ticket --> Permission{Dispatch fence ever published?} Permission -->|Yes or exit not proven| Preserve[Preserve uncertainty] Permission -->|No| Check[Recheck detached job, intent and absence of execution evidence] Check -->|All checks pass| Unstarted[Publish failed-to-start or confirmed cancellation with executed false] Check -->|Any check fails| Preserve Validate -->|Invalid evidence| Error[Record reconciliation failure and retain claims]

Without a receipt, the helper requires a matching scoped ticket and either the live reaper's observed PID exit or a definitively dead recorded process identity. Legacy tickets or uncertain liveness cannot clear claims. A dispatch fence keeps the outcome uncertain even when no command PID survived. The final transaction also refuses to rewrite a terminal job or a job with execution, command-PID or start-time evidence. A previously requested cancellation becomes confirmed only on this proven-before-dispatch path; otherwise the job fails to start.

Bounded shutdown and lease release

close first enters QUIESCING, wakes state waiters and closes worker IPC. It asks the background checkpointer to stop and waits up to five seconds for that thread. This is separate from stopping the external command owners described by the worker protocol.

sequenceDiagram participant Caller participant Hub as State hub participant Writer as Background checkpointer participant Final as Shutdown continuation participant Leases as Root, node and replay leases Caller->>Hub: close(checkpoint=True) Hub->>Hub: QUIESCING, notify waiters and close IPC Hub->>Writer: Stop and join for up to five seconds alt Background writer still running Hub->>Final: Start daemon waiting for existing writer Hub-->>Caller: False Writer-->>Final: Existing writer exits Final->>Leases: Mark CLOSED and release leases Note over Final,Leases: This branch does not start another final checkpoint else Background writer ended and final checkpoint is requested and dirty Hub->>Final: Start final checkpoint thread alt Final attempt ends within five seconds Final->>Final: Write or record exception class on failure Final->>Leases: Mark CLOSED and release leases Hub-->>Caller: True even if final write failed else Final attempt still running after five seconds Hub-->>Caller: False Final->>Final: Eventually finish write or record its failure Final->>Leases: Mark CLOSED and release leases after attempt ends end else No final write required Hub->>Leases: Mark CLOSED and release leases Hub-->>Caller: True end

The return value reports completion of this shutdown path. True does not certify that the final write succeeded: that thread records an error and releases leases in finally. False means a continuation still owns the leases; a replacement cannot overlap the physical writer. If the background writer exceeded its wait, the continuation only joins that writer and releases ownership, even if a newer revision remains dirty. Callers requiring a durable drain must separately verify committed revision and persistence diagnostics. Calling close on an already closed or inherited hub returns without starting this sequence.

Evidence and limits of this review

RAM-state tests cover owner sharing, copy isolation, transaction conflicts, legacy imports, replay retention and process/fork ownership. Fault tests exercise manifest publication boundaries, newer dirty revisions, partial fence writes, final directory-sync failure and signed completion. Operation tests cover event order, limits, candidate indexes and isolated offline bundle/repair commands. These use temporary state, synthetic workers and local transport fixtures. They do not certify all native filesystem/ACL environments or a production crash. The bounded shutdown branches above are traced directly from hub.close and Checkpointer.close; the cited suites do not inject a late shutdown writer.
